## Instructor-facing script

This is **your** teaching script for Day 1, not a student handout. It gives
the running order, timings, demo code to project, and exercise prompts.
Students work from the book (chapters 1, 2, 5, 6, 10) and the data files
distributed on USB.

**Pattern per section** (your decision):
1. Short intro — you set up the concept
2. Students try — on their own machines, before you've shown them
3. Demo — you work it live, explaining as you go
4. Exercise — closes the section, students apply what they just saw
:::

## Before you start the room

Pre-session checklist (10 min before 09:00):

- [ ] Projector works, your screen is at or near 150% zoom (RStudio text readable from the back)
- [ ] USB sticks with corpus data ready to hand round at Break 1
- [ ] Your R-4-HASS repo clone is on your laptop, logged into GitHub, PAT in credential store
- [ ] A pinned browser tab on <https://github.com/MartinSchweinberger/R-4-HASS> and one on <https://ladal.edu.au/>
- [ ] Pre-prepared bits/notes for the inevitable "I don't have R installed" / "my Git says command not found" cases

## Student install state — assume partial compliance

Pre-course email asked students to install R, RStudio, Quarto, Git, and
create a GitHub account before Day 1. Realistic compliance from 35
students: ~25 fully compliant, ~7 partially, ~3 nothing done. Have a
"catch-up corner" plan — a visible place where students who are behind
work alongside the rest. Don't block the whole room on their issues.

## 09:00–09:10 · Opening (10 min)

Short. Students have been in talks before; the first 10 min signals how
this day will run.

**What to cover:**

- Who you are, one sentence on what the course is for
- Four-day arc (foundations → text analytics → statistics & modelling → publishing)
- Where the materials live: the book (point at the GitHub URL on screen),
  the per-day scripts (today's is this file), the data on USB
- Prüfungsleistung reminder (one line each for Hausarbeit route vs
  Quarto-document route)
- The daily rhythm: short intro, you try, I demo, exercises; two breaks + lunch
- End-of-day goal: every student leaves with a working R project, a
  public GitHub repo, imported real linguistic data, and a saved plot

**Do not cover:**

- Why R vs SPSS tangent (lose 5 min, gain nothing)
- Full tour of the book TOC (point at it, move on)
- History of R, tidyverse philosophy, functional-vs-imperative — any of this

## 09:10–10:10 · §1. RStudio, projects, packages (60 min)

**Aim.** Every student has an R project called R-4-HASS, a `scripts/`
folder, a running `day1.R`, and the four core packages loaded without
errors.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 1 (`01-r_intro.qmd`), §§1–3.

### 1.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points to make:

- RStudio ≠ R. R is the engine; RStudio is the dashboard. If RStudio
  crashes, your R work is still safe (saved scripts and data).
- The four panes: script editor (top-left), console (bottom-left),
  environment (top-right), files/plots/help (bottom-right).
- An R **project** is a self-contained working directory. One project
  per piece of work. The `.Rproj` file sets the working directory
  automatically — you never need `setwd()`.
- A **package** is other people's R code. Install once (`install.packages()`),
  load every session (`library()`).
- `<-` vs `=`: both work for assignment; `<-` is community convention.

Don't labour the assignment operator discussion. One sentence, move on.

### 1.2 Students try (15 min)

Prompt on screen (leave it up):

> 1. Open RStudio. Point at each of the four panes in turn.
> 2. **File → New Project → New Directory**, call it `R-4-HASS`. Save it
>    somewhere you'll find again (your `Documents` folder is fine).
> 3. In the Files pane, create a new folder called `scripts`.
> 4. **File → New File → R Script**, save it as `scripts/day1.R`.
> 5. Type `1 + 1` on the first line. Run it with Ctrl/Cmd + Enter.
> 6. Below that: `my_name <- "your name"`. Run it. Check Environment pane.

Walk the room. Expect: students without R installed, students with
RStudio opening on a non-English locale, students whose `Documents` is
synced to OneDrive and so the project refuses to save. Flag these to
the catch-up corner; don't stop.

### 1.3 Demo (20 min)

Project on screen:

```{r demo-1-3, eval=TRUE}
# Where am I?
getwd()

# Make sure the four core packages are installed
# (Pre-course email asked students to do this already — this is a check)
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "readxl", "flextable"))

# Load them
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, ggplot2, readr, tidyr, stringr, forcats, purrr, tibble
library(here)        # robust file paths
library(readxl)      # Excel files
library(flextable)   # nice tables for reports

# What does `here` give us?
here::here()              # project root
here::here("scripts")     # project root + /scripts

# Scope operator — "this function from this package"
# Useful when two packages export the same name
stringr::str_length("Blockseminar")
```

Talking points while typing (not after):

- `tidyverse` is a bundle — one call loads eight packages
- `library(here)` + `here::here()` means your script works on anyone's machine
- `::` is a safety net; use it in production code and when you want to be
  explicit about which package a function comes from

### 1.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.** Add three more folders to your `R-4-HASS` project: `data/`,
> `figures/`, and `output/`. In your `day1.R`, write code that uses
> `here::here()` to print the full path to each of these folders.
> Save the script.
>
> **Bonus.** Install one additional package of your choice from
> `install.packages("<name>")` and load it.

Common slips to watch for:

- Students creating folders in Finder/Explorer, then not seeing them in
  the Files pane → press F5 or click the refresh icon
- Students pasting `install.packages()` into the script and running it
  every time → tell them to comment it out: `# install.packages(...)`
- `here()` without `library(here)` → good teaching moment on load-then-use

**Hand off to §2:** *"You now have a project. Next we're going to put
it on GitHub so you can back it up, share it, and — on Day 4 — turn it
into a public website."*

## 10:25–11:55 · §2. Git & GitHub setup (90 min)

**Aim.** Every student has their R-4-HASS project connected to a public
GitHub repository and has pushed at least one commit from RStudio.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10 (`10-publish.qmd`), §§ on Git basics
and PAT setup. (Note: Ch 10 is publishing-focused — the Git basics are
background for that chapter, not the main thrust. For today, we're
using the Git parts and skipping the Quarto-publishing parts.)

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the highest-risk section of Day 1

Set a hard timebox. If a student is still blocked at 11:40, tell them
to finish at home, and move on. The goal is that most students have
a repo online by lunch — not that every student does.
:::

### 2.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- **Git** is a tool on your laptop that tracks changes to files.
  **GitHub** is a website that stores Git repositories online.
  The two are not the same thing. Git works without GitHub; GitHub
  without Git is just file storage.
- A **commit** is a snapshot of your project at a point in time, with a
  message explaining what changed. A **push** sends your commits to
  GitHub. A **pull** gets other people's commits down.
- Authentication: HTTPS + Personal Access Token (PAT). SSH keys are
  cleaner but harder to set up for 35 beginners in 90 minutes. We use PAT.
- A PAT is like a password with scopes. It's shown ONCE. If you lose it,
  generate a new one.

Draw on the whiteboard: *your laptop (local repo)* ↔ *GitHub (remote repo)*,
with push/pull arrows. Keep it on the board.

### 2.2 Students try (25 min)

Prompt on screen:

> **A. Verify Git is installed.** Open the Terminal tab in RStudio
> (Tools → Terminal → New Terminal). Type:
>
> ```bash
> git --version
> ```
>
> You should see something like `git version 2.43.0`. If not,
> flag this and visit catch-up corner.
>
> **B. Tell Git who you are.** In Terminal:
>
> ```bash
> git config --global user.name "Your Name"
> git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
> ```
>
> Use the email you used to sign up for GitHub.
>
> **C. Create an empty repo on GitHub.**
>
> 1. Go to <https://github.com> and sign in.
> 2. Click **New** (green button, top-left after sign-in).
> 3. Repository name: `R-4-HASS`.
> 4. Public. Do NOT add a README, .gitignore, or license (we have one locally).
> 5. Click **Create repository**.
> 6. Leave this page open — the next step uses the URL shown.

### 2.3 Demo (25 min)

PAT generation — do this with students, step by step:

> **D. Generate a Personal Access Token.**
>
> 1. On GitHub, click your profile picture → **Settings**
> 2. Scroll down the sidebar → **Developer settings**
> 3. **Personal access tokens** → **Tokens (classic)**
> 4. **Generate new token** → **Generate new token (classic)**
> 5. Note: `R-4-HASS laptop` (or similar)
> 6. Expiration: 90 days is fine
> 7. Scopes: tick `repo` (that's the whole top block)
> 8. **Generate token**
> 9. **Copy the token immediately — this is the only time it is shown.**
>    Paste it into a text file as a backup until it's stored by Git.

Then wire the local R-4-HASS up to the new empty GitHub repo. In Terminal
inside the R-4-HASS project:

```bash
# Initialise git tracking in the current folder
git init

# Stage everything currently in the folder
git add .

# Create the first commit
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Rename default branch to main (if not already)
git branch -M main

# Connect this local repo to the GitHub remote
# (replace USERNAME with the student's GitHub username)
git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/R-4-HASS.git

# Push to GitHub — this will prompt for username + PAT
git push -u origin main
```

When prompted:

- Username: your GitHub username
- Password: paste the PAT (NOT your GitHub login password)

The PAT will be stored by the OS credential manager (Git Credential
Manager on Windows, Keychain on macOS, libsecret on Linux). Students
should only need to paste once.

Refresh the GitHub repo page in the browser — files should appear.

### 2.4 Exercise (25 min)

> **Task.** Make a small change and push it from RStudio (not Terminal).
>
> 1. Open `day1.R` in RStudio.
> 2. Add a comment at the top: `# Day 1 — my first commit from RStudio`.
> 3. Save the file.
> 4. In the top-right pane, click the **Git** tab.
>    (If no Git tab: Tools → Project Options → Git/SVN → set version
>    control to Git, restart RStudio.)
> 5. Tick the box next to `day1.R` under "Staged".
> 6. Click **Commit**. In the message box, type: `Add header comment`.
>    Click **Commit** again.
> 7. Click **Push** (green up arrow).
> 8. Refresh your GitHub repo page in the browser. The change should be there.

Common failure modes and quick fixes:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `git: command not found` | Git not on PATH | Reinstall from git-scm.com, tick "add to PATH" |
| No Git tab in RStudio | Project not Git-tracked, or RStudio needs restart | Tools → Project Options → Git/SVN, then restart |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | Trying SSH not HTTPS | Switch remote to HTTPS: `git remote set-url origin https://...` |
| PAT paste shows asterisks only, won't accept | Terminal hiding paste for security | Try Ctrl+Shift+V on Windows, Cmd+V on Mac — it's working |
| `rejected — fetch first` | Repo was created with README on GitHub | Delete the GitHub repo, recreate without README, retry |

**Hand off:** *"Everyone with a repo online, raise a hand. [Count.] Those
without one, grab me or sit with the catch-up corner over lunch. We
move on."*

## 12:55–14:10 · §3. Data in R — types and import (75 min)

**Aim.** Every student imports CSV, TSV, and Excel files from the USB
data into their project and can describe what came in with `str()`,
`glimpse()`, `summary()`.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 2 (`02-data_loading.qmd`).

### 3.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- **Vectors** are the basic R object: `c(1, 2, 3)`, `c("a", "b", "c")`.
- **Factors** are vectors where each value is one of a set of levels.
  Useful for categorical variables (gender, register, speaker).
- **Data frames** are tables where each column is a vector of the same
  length. **Tibbles** are the tidyverse version: better print output
  and fewer surprises.
- File formats: CSV is the lingua franca. TSV when commas are in your
  data. Excel is common in humanities but has encoding and date pitfalls.
  `.rda` / `.RData` are R's own format — fastest to read, R-only.
- `readr::read_csv()` reads much faster than base R's `read.csv()`,
  and returns a tibble.

Draw on the whiteboard: a tibble = rows (observations) × columns
(variables). Keep it there.

### 3.2 Students try (20 min)

Prompt on screen:

> **A. Build a tibble by hand.** In `day1.R`:
>
> ```r
> speakers <- tibble::tibble(
>   speaker  = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04", "S05"),
>   age      = c(23, 45, 67, 34, 29),
>   register = c("spoken", "written", "spoken", "spoken", "written"),
>   tokens   = c(1203, 847, 2104, 1567, 923)
> )
>
> speakers
> ```
>
> **B. Inspect it:**
>
> ```r
> str(speakers)        # structure
> dplyr::glimpse(speakers)  # tidyverse glimpse
> summary(speakers)    # five-number summary + factor counts
> head(speakers, 3)    # top 3 rows
> ```
>
> **C. One question:** what does `speakers$register` give you back?
> Run it and see.

### 3.3 Demo (25 min)

Move the data from USB into `data/` first (show them):

```{r demo-3-3, eval=TRUE}
# Where should the data be?
here::here("data")

# Load the main test files
testdat_csv  <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "testdat.csv"))
testdat_tsv  <- readr::read_tsv(here::here("data", "testdat.txt"))
testdat_xlsx <- readxl::read_excel(here::here("data", "testdat.xlsx"))

# Compare them — they should look similar if the files were created in parallel
dplyr::glimpse(testdat_csv)
dplyr::glimpse(testdat_tsv)
dplyr::glimpse(testdat_xlsx)

# Inspect in more detail
summary(testdat_csv)

# What if the encoding is wrong?
# You see "Mßller" instead of "Müller"? Try specifying UTF-8:
testdat_csv2 <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "testdat.csv"),
  locale = readr::locale(encoding = "UTF-8")
)

# Save a processed version back out
readr::write_csv(testdat_csv, here::here("output", "testdat_clean.csv"))
```

Talking points:

- `read_csv()` tells you what it did — read the specification output;
  don't ignore it
- Use `here::here()` consistently; never `read_csv("data/testdat.csv")`
- Encoding problems are the single most common import issue in
  humanities data — if the text looks garbled, it's an encoding issue
  nine times out of ten
- `.rda` files are loaded with `readRDS()` (single object) or `load()`
  (names appear in environment); show which the LADAL files use

### 3.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.**
>
> 1. Import `testdat2.csv` into R.
> 2. Use `glimpse()` to describe its structure.
> 3. Save it as an Excel file in your `output/` folder using
>    `writexl::write_xlsx()` (install `writexl` first if needed).
> 4. Open the Excel file to verify it looks right.
>
> **Reflect.** What was the easiest format to work with, and why?

## 14:25–15:25 · §4. Data manipulation with `dplyr` (60 min)

**Aim.** Every student uses `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `arrange()`,
`group_by()` + `summarise()` on a real dataset to answer a question.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 5 (`05-tables.qmd`).

### 4.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- `dplyr` has five "verbs" that cover 90% of data wrangling:
  - `filter()` — keep rows that match a condition
  - `select()` — keep columns you want
  - `mutate()` — add or change columns
  - `arrange()` — sort rows
  - `summarise()` — collapse rows into summary statistics
- `group_by()` is the modifier that makes `summarise()` operate
  per-group rather than over the whole table.
- The pipe `|>` (or `%>%`) means "take what's on the left, feed it
  into the function on the right as the first argument". Reads as
  "then".

### 4.2 Students try (15 min)

Prompt (dataset here is the one they imported in §3; adjust to your
provided data):

> Using `testdat_csv` (or whichever one you prefer):
>
> ```r
> # Keep only rows where some column meets a condition
> testdat_csv |>
>   dplyr::filter(SomeVariable == "SomeValue")
>
> # Keep only certain columns
> testdat_csv |>
>   dplyr::select(SomeVariable, AnotherVariable)
>
> # Try one on your own: filter + select combined
> ```
>
> Replace `SomeVariable` and `SomeValue` with real column names and
> values from your data. Use `glimpse()` to remind yourself what's there.

### 4.3 Demo (20 min)

Build up a pipeline, line by line, explaining each verb:

```{r demo-4-3, eval=TRUE}
# Starting from the raw tibble
testdat_csv |>
  dplyr::glimpse()

# Filter: just one subset
testdat_csv |>
  dplyr::filter(Age > 30)

# Add filter + select + arrange
testdat_csv |>
  dplyr::filter(Age > 30) |>
  dplyr::select(Speaker, Age, Register) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Age))

# mutate — add a derived column
testdat_csv |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_group = dplyr::case_when(
      Age < 30 ~ "young",
      Age < 60 ~ "middle",
      TRUE     ~ "older"
    )
  )

# group_by + summarise — the classic group analysis
testdat_csv |>
  dplyr::group_by(Register) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n       = dplyr::n(),
    mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

(Note: `Age`, `Speaker`, `Register` are placeholders — swap for your
dataset's actual column names.)

Talking points:

- Build the pipeline incrementally — add one verb, run, check output,
  add the next. Don't write the whole chain and hope.
- `|>` is R 4.1+. `%>%` is tidyverse's older pipe — they're nearly
  equivalent. Students will see both in the wild.
- `.groups = "drop"` silences a benign warning — explain once, move on.
- `dplyr::` prefix is for teaching clarity; in practice, students will
  write `filter()` after `library(dplyr)`.

### 4.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.** Answer these three questions about the dataset using `dplyr`:
>
> 1. How many observations are in each register?
> 2. What is the mean of some numeric variable, broken down by group?
> 3. Which 5 rows have the highest value on some variable?
>
> Write each as a single `|>` pipeline. Save each in `day1.R` with a
> comment above explaining what it does.

(Rephrase these to match the actual columns of the dataset students
have.)

## 15:25–16:15 · §5. First `ggplot2` (50 min)

**Aim.** Every student creates a bar chart and a scatter plot with
`ggplot2`, customises labels, and saves one plot to `figures/` with
`ggsave()`.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 6 (`06-data_viz_intro.qmd`).

### 5.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- `ggplot2` is built on the **grammar of graphics**: every plot is
  (data) + (aesthetic mapping) + (geometric layer) + (optional
  statistics, scales, facets, themes).
- The template:

  ```r
  ggplot(data = <DATA>, aes(x = <X>, y = <Y>, colour = <GROUP>)) +
    geom_<TYPE>() +
    labs(title = "...", x = "...", y = "...") +
    theme_bw()
  ```

- Layers are added with `+`, NOT `|>`. This trips everyone up once.
- `aes()` maps variables → visual properties. Anything inside `aes()`
  is data-driven; anything outside is fixed.

### 5.2 Students try (10 min)

> Make a basic bar chart of the counts of some categorical variable:
>
> ```r
> ggplot(data = testdat_csv, aes(x = Register)) +
>   geom_bar()
> ```
>
> Then try a scatter plot of two numeric variables:
>
> ```r
> ggplot(data = testdat_csv, aes(x = Age, y = Tokens)) +
>   geom_point()
> ```
>
> Adjust column names to match your data.

### 5.3 Demo (15 min)

Build up a publication-ready plot:

```{r demo-5-3, eval=TRUE}
# Start simple
p <- ggplot(data = testdat_csv, aes(x = Age, y = Tokens))
p

# Add a geom
p + geom_point()

# Colour by group
p + geom_point(aes(colour = Register))

# Add a smoother
p +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Register)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

# Labels and theme
p +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Register), size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Tokens by speaker age",
    subtitle = "Linear fit by register",
    x        = "Speaker age (years)",
    y        = "Tokens produced",
    colour   = "Register"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Save it
ggsave(
  filename = here::here("figures", "tokens-by-age.png"),
  width    = 7,
  height   = 4.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

Talking points:

- Build the plot in layers; print after each addition
- `theme_bw()` + explicit axis labels = 90% of publication quality
- Save as PNG for most purposes; PDF if going into LaTeX
- Default `ggsave` dimensions are too big for most needs; always set
  `width` and `height`

### 5.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.**
>
> 1. Make a boxplot of a numeric variable by a categorical variable.
> 2. Customise with `labs()` — give it a proper title, axis labels, caption.
> 3. Change the theme to `theme_minimal()` or `theme_classic()`.
> 4. Save to `figures/` as a PNG, 7 × 4 inches, 300 dpi.
> 5. Commit and push the figure to GitHub (practice the full cycle).

## Appendix A — Risk register for Day 1

| # | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Students without R/RStudio installed | High | Catch-up corner, don't block |
| 2 | §2 PAT confusion with 35 students | High | Set hard timebox, "finish at home" fallback |
| 3 | §2 overruns, pushing §3 into lunch | Medium | Cut §2 exercise to 15 min if §2.3 ran long |
| 4 | USB data distribution is slow | Medium | Hand out at Break 1, not during §3 |
| 5 | OneDrive/corporate laptop lockdown | Low–Medium | Have alternative install path for Git ready |
| 6 | Encoding issues breaking imports | Medium | Explicit UTF-8 locale in demo code |
| 7 | ggplot2 `+` vs `|>` confusion | High | Call this out explicitly in §5.1 |

## Appendix B — If you fall behind

If §2 (Git/GitHub) overruns to 12:15:

- Shorten §3 Intro to 10 min (skip the vectors/factors discussion, go
  straight to tibbles)
- Shorten §4 Exercise to 10 min (two questions instead of three)
- Keep §5 as is — the publication-quality plot is a satisfying ending

If §2 is still running at 12:30:

- Declare Git/GitHub "finish over lunch and after Day 2"
- Skip to §3; those with repos online can commit as they go, others
  can commit at end of Day 2

## Appendix C — Data files assumed in `data/`

For Day 1 you need (copy from LADAL `data_loading` tutorial folder,
listed in R-4-HASS README §1):

- `testdat.csv`, `testdat2.csv` — small demo CSV
- `testdat.txt` — TSV version
- `testdat.xlsx` — Excel version

For §4 and §5 you may wish to swap in a richer linguistic dataset — the
`pvd.rda` corpus used by Ch 6 is a good candidate once students have
`load()`ed it. Check before Day 1 that these files are on the USB sticks.
